name: Workwear style

lead: Workwear style borrows clothing designed for manual trades, such as denim jackets, chore coats, overalls, canvas trousers, flannels and boots, and wears it as everyday fashion. The payoff is a sturdy, masculine, put-together silhouette from heavy fabrics that hold their shape and tend to look better with wear.

The look has roots in 19th-century trade uniforms and moved into fashion through subcultures in the 1980s, then streetwear and heritage menswear in the 21st century. No studies address it as a style approach; the research that surfaces under the term concerns occupational protective clothing.

paras: People build outfits from a few staples: raw or dark denim, a chore or work jacket, a chambray or flannel shirt, canvas or twill pants and sturdy boots. Palettes are usually earthy and muted. The pieces are often worn for years and buyers value fabric weight, reinforced stitching and fit.
Little physical risk. Heavy fabrics can be warm and stiff at first, and boxy cuts can swamp slighter frames if oversized. Fit and proportion determine the result.

angle.text: Wearers use workwear pieces to get a structured, rugged silhouette and a coherent outfit from a small set of staples. Denim, canvas and boots read as sturdy and are easy to coordinate.

lead: Workwear style is the use of garments originally made for manual labour as everyday fashion. Wikipedia describes workwear as clothing chosen for durability and safety that often signalled a worker's trade [1].

For looks, workwear pieces supply structure: heavy twill, denim and canvas hold a clean shoulder and straight leg, and the earth-toned palette keeps outfits simple. Fashion adoption moved from 1980s subcultures that took donkey jackets and boots, to 21st-century streetwear and hipster culture featuring denim jackets, flannels, chambray, raw denim and work boots [1].
Research found under the term is about occupational garments, such as protective clothing ergonomics and thermal comfort, rather than fashion outcomes [2][3].
infobox: Denim, chore coat, overalls, canvas pants, boots

paras: Workwear garments emphasise durability: heavy fabrics such as denim, cotton duck and twill, and reinforced stitching at stress points [4]. Examples across history include British donkey jackets and corduroy, maritime denim and peacoats, American railroad overalls, lumberjack plaid and mechanic's boiler suits [1].

Workwear emerged with industrialisation in the 19th century [4]. Wikipedia notes 1980s British subcultures adopting donkey jackets and Doc Martens, later bands adopting flat caps as working-class identity, and in the 21st century workwear influencing streetwear and hipster culture [1]. Japan developed its own workwear lineage in the early 20th century by combining Japanese and European styles [1].
Workwear is discussed in style circles as a way to look rugged and put together with few items. Because the garments are cut for movement they tend to be roomy, so fit adjustments matter.

No studies found on workwear as a fashion style. Related occupational research examines protective clothing: reviews of heat stress from protective garments [2], clothing insulation under wind and movement [5] and mining workwear design [3].
